lines: Here's the big idea, friend. Jesus tells about a manager who's about to lose his job, and the story flat-out calls him the dishonest manager (Luke 16:8). He knocks his master's bills down, a hundred measures of olive oil to fifty, so people will welcome him into their homes once he's out (Luke 16:4-6).

And the master commends him, because he had acted shrewdly (Luke 16:8). Not for being honest. For seeing the end coming and getting ready for it. Then the line right after says, "the sons of this age are more shrewd in dealing with their own kind than are the sons of light." (Luke 16:8) Baker, that's your coworker with a five-year plan, while I'm over here still looking for my other oven mitt.

So Jesus says to use worldly wealth to make friends for yourselves, so that "when it is gone," they will welcome you into eternal dwellings (Luke 16:9). WHEN it is gone. Not if. Money runs out. So spend the stuff that runs out on the stuff that lasts forever.

And no, Jesus is not handing out gold stars for creative math. He says whoever is dishonest with very little will also be dishonest with much (Luke 16:10). Then He asks it straight: if you haven't been faithful with worldly wealth, who will entrust you with true riches (Luke 16:11)?
Friend, the small stuff is the practice round for the big stuff (Luke 16:10-12). I should know. I stamped crooked for YEARS before anybody handed me cookies for the Marriage Supper.

Then Jesus lands it: "You cannot serve both God and money." (Luke 16:13) Money can be a tool in your hand. It cannot be the boss of your heart. One master. This is NOT a job share. And Jesus isn't done talking about money yet.
